label: PLAIN:baseline
name: Append-only errata with ski-rental compaction
mech: This runs on the client only and works with any API. Never change content that has already been sent. Express a middle edit, a changed tool output or an insertion as a short tagged erratum at the end of the prompt, for example "[supersedes tool_result #17]: …". Sort documents into a fixed order, such as by content hash, and serialize JSON with sorted keys, so that reordering becomes an exact prefix match. Do a real in-place rewrite (compaction) only when the running cost of the errata reaches the one-time cost of rewriting the suffix. That is the ski-rental rule, and it costs at most 2x the best possible schedule. With Anthropic's prices (cache write 1.25x the base input price, cache read 0.1x), an erratum of e tokens placed after an edit at position p in an N-token context breaks even with a rewrite only after T* = (1.25(N−p) − 1.25e)/(0.1e) turns. For N=100k, p=50k and e=500 that is 1,238 turns; for an edit near the end (p=90k, e=2k) it is 50 turns. So the erratum is almost always cheaper, and compaction is driven by the context-window limit, not by cost. In a 50-turn synthetic agent replay with 2k-token tool outputs and an earlier tool output changing every 5 turns, the token hit rate rose from 92.9% to 99.75% and billed input fell from 604k to 365k units (−40%). Tokens are exactly what the model would compute, so the KV state matches full recomputation exactly. The only quality risk is semantic: stale text stays in the prompt next to its correction.
value: This gives a hit rate near 100% for edits, tool outputs and insertions, and for reordering of document sets that repeat, at no infrastructure cost. In the replay it cut input cost by about 40% against append-and-edit prefix caching. It extends Manus's "append-only context" guidance with a cost-optimal rule for when to compact. Quality has to be tested as an A/B on agent traces, for example SWE-bench success rate and needle-in-a-haystack tests with superseded facts. That test needs a real model and was not run here.

label: PLAIN:baseline
name: Hole-punch deletes via block-table edits
mech: This needs your own serving stack or provider-side changes, and would be exposed as a new API operation such as `delete_span(id)`. The most common mid-prompt change in agents is deletion: clearing old tool results or compaction. Provider "context editing" features currently throw away the cached prefix at that point. Instead, drop the deleted span's paged-KV blocks from the request's block table and keep every later block as it is. New tokens either continue after a gap in position IDs (PyramidKV-style) or have their keys rotated back into a dense range with a delta RoPE rotation (HERMES and KV Packet rotation). The cost is zero recompute and zero extra memory, and the freed blocks are returned to the pool. The hit rate on the remaining tokens is 100%, but the result is not exactly what full recomputation gives. Tokens after the hole still carry information they absorbed from the deleted span. That is often harmless or even useful for compaction, but harmful when the deleted text was wrong, so pair it with an erratum from Idea 1. Prior art: llama.cpp context shift, and KV-eviction methods (StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV), which use the same mechanism to choose tokens heuristically. What is new is driving it from an explicit edit request and billing it as a cache hit.
value: Deletions and compaction become cache hits at 0.1x instead of a rewrite of the whole suffix at 1.25x, a 12.5x cheaper suffix. Quality test: KL divergence and top-1 agreement of next-token distributions against full recomputation on real agent traces, measured with the gap and the rotation variants. This needs a real model.

label: PLAIN:baseline
name: Segment cache with boundary recompute
mech: This runs on your own stack, for example LMCache's CacheBlend in vLLM, or provider-side. Cache the KV of each document or tool output on its own, keyed by content hash. Compute it after the real shared system prompt (APE's "shared prefix") so it differs less from in-context KV. When reusing a segment at a new position, rotate its RoPE positions and recompute only the tokens whose KV deviates most. CacheBlend recomputes about 15% of tokens and reports a 2.2–3.3x faster time-to-first-token with same-quality answers on RAG question answering. EPIC recomputes only the first few tokens of each chunk (about 32 of 512 tokens, roughly 6%, so about 94% effective hit) and reports up to 8x faster time-to-first-token with "negligible" loss. Add a deviation gate: if the layer-1 deviation (the CacheBlend signal) is above a threshold, fall back to exact recompute. Covered cases: reordering, insertions and changed segments. Only the changed segment and its boundary tokens are recomputed. Storage grows with one KV copy per unique segment: 320 KB per token for Llama-3-70B in BF16, 69 KB per token for DeepSeek-V3's MLA. Latency adds a PCIe load of about 6.6 s per 1M tokens of 70B BF16 KV.
value: About 85–94% of non-prefix tokens are served from cache, and prefill compute falls about 3–7x against exact prefix caching on RAG and reordered workloads. Quality is not exact. The SIGMOD'26 Fusion-RAG paper and AgentKVShift report a remaining gap on multi-hop and agent-memory tasks. Quality test: run it against full recomputation on 2WikiMQA and MuSiQue (multi-hop QA), on LongBench, and on real agent traces.

label: PLAIN:baseline
name: Storage-priced retention, not token-priced hits
mech: This runs on your own stack or provider-side. At high hit rates, the real cost of a hit is storing the KV, not computing it. Recomputing a token of a 70B model costs about $0.175 per 1M tokens (H100 at $2/h, 45% compute utilization). Holding the same KV for one hour costs about $8.2 per 1M tokens in GPU memory (HBM), $1.6 in CPU RAM (DRAM) and $0.07 on NVMe SSD. So a 1h DRAM-resident cache only pays off if the context is reused about every 6 minutes. NVMe pays off down to about one reuse per 2.5 h. FP8 halves these costs, and MLA models cut them about 4.6x. Retention per prefix should therefore use a ski-rental rule too: keep the KV in a tier while (expected reuses) × (recompute cost) is greater than storage cost × time. The default for long-tail sessions should be NVMe with a long TTL plus MLA or FP8 KV, not GPU memory.
value: This is what makes a hit rate near 100% affordable, at a storage cost about 20x lower than DRAM. It also shows that pushing hit rate and price down together is limited by storage. Prior art is tiered caching (Mooncake, LMCache, HiCache), which per earlier runs gains only about 1.2x over GPU-only prefix caching. The addition is cost-based eviction per prefix.

label: V5:repair
name: Context-length-gated turn collapsing
mech: The anchor is that the agent stops to observe only when the expected value of seeing the result is worth one more full-context read, priced at C×0.1×p (C is the current context length, p the base input price). The threshold therefore tightens as C grows: early turns observe freely, and turns after about 20–40k tokens are folded into multi-step scripts (k=3 steps per turn). Each script filters its tool outputs down to the lines needed for the next decision, so less text enters the context and every later read shrinks. The design changes are these. Only read-only or idempotent tools are folded. A script stops early as soon as an expectation check fails. Folded batches longer than 5 minutes use the 1-hour cache TTL. On a 40-turn session the gate gives 1.48× and the gate plus 50% filtering gives 1.81×. On a 150-turn session, where reads are 75% of cost, the gate gives 2.02× and gate plus filtering gives 2.42×.
value: About 2.0–2.4× cheaper per long agent task than the plain cached agent loop. That compares with 1.20× for CodeAct's measured 30% turn cut and 0.83× for observation masking once cache rewrites are paid.

label: V5:repair
name: Floating depth-1 override ledger
mech: Anchor: an edit never rewrites earlier context; it is sent as an appended patch, so the cached prefix stays byte-identical. Repair: patches no longer pile up in history. The client keeps one deduplicated ledger with a single entry per stable section or state key ("§4 now reads…", "plan.status = …"). It places the ledger after the last cache breakpoint, right after the current question, and drops it from the history it sends next turn. Each turn therefore re-pays only the ledger at 1.0× plus the reply tokens. Each key only ever has the original plus one override, so the depth-driven interference measured by PI-LLM and DKI stays at depth 1. The ledger is folded into the document when its spend exceeds one rewrite from the earliest edited position, when it passes 10% of the context, or for free on any turn where the cache has already expired. In the model, a 150k-token agent context with 8k of mutable state at the front (40 calls, 20 state edits) costs $0.0735 per request against $0.336 for inline rewriting. That is 4.6× cheaper and within 6% of the no-edit floor. A 25k-token document with 10 questions and 3 edits comes out 1.46× cheaper with the 10% cap.
value: When the same state or section is edited repeatedly on a hosted API, cost per request falls 2.6–4.6× against inline rewriting, at the same cost as the patch chain coding agents already use (within 4–8%) but with override depth held at 1 instead of the chain's 3–7.

label: V5:repair
name: Cost-optimal patch folding
mech: Anchor: edits become structured appended patches, and a full rewrite runs only when the patches cost more than one fresh write. Repair: the fold rule is now ski-rental, which is guaranteed to cost at most 2× what the best possible fold timing would have cost. The client folds once the patches' cumulative extra reads reach the cost of rewriting from the earliest patched position, not from the start of the document. Two triggers are new: a second edit to the same key forces a fold (depth cap 1, because the PI-LLM/DKI evidence shows accuracy on the latest value falls as updates accumulate), and folding is free on any request that would miss the cache anyway (gap longer than the TTL), since that request rewrites everything regardless. Documents are given stable section IDs when they are loaded so patches can address sections. In the model this gives 1.52× (25k document, 10 questions, 3 edits) and 2.66× (120k copilot document, 30 questions, 15 edits) against inline rewriting. The token-weighted hit rate is 96.4%, which is every reusable token; inline gets about 71%.
value: Document sessions with scattered edits on hosted APIs get 1.5–2.7× lower cost per question than inline rewriting, with no more than one override per section. The gain shrinks to about 1.2–1.4× when 30% of gaps between turns exceed the cache TTL.

label: V6:improve_g1
name: Popularity-first exact-prefix document ordering
mech: Remove the blending stage, which is the part later papers dispute. Order retrieved documents by descending global retrieval frequency, using an online counter with ties broken by ID. Put the system prompt first and the question last. Every reuse is then an exact prefix hit, so the reused KV equals what full recomputation would give for that order. The only quality effect is the reorder itself. Stable-RAG reports that answers change with document order even under 1k tokens. To test it, run the same retrieved sets in relevance order and in popularity order and compare F1/EM and the spread across permutations (needs a real model). I replayed the same setup as FACT 5 (100k chunks, top-5, Zipf). Exact document-token reuse is 0.400, 0.546 and 0.768 at Zipf 1.05, 1.2 and 1.5. Hash order gives 0.152, 0.229 and 0.503; relevance (random) order gives 0.166, 0.249 and 0.425. A cache-aware trie-greedy order like CacheWeaver's gives 0.403, 0.548 and 0.769, the same as the counter. Because the counter needs no view of the cache, the method runs client-side through a third-party API. Under Anthropic's multipliers, the per-request bill is 1.17x, 1.35x and 1.78x cheaper than the usual practice of sending documents uncached. Caching documents only pays once reuse is above 0.217; hash order plus cache_control actually loses (0.95x). Self-hosted, the gain is 1.17x, 1.26x and 1.43x. Limits: per-document breakpoints (at most 4 per request), a 1,024-token minimum prefix, traffic arriving within the 5-minute TTL, and an LRU cap of 20k tree nodes that costs at most 1.4 points of reuse. Covers document reordering only.
value: 1.2–1.8x per request against the best current API practice, without approximating any KV, and it works for API users. This is the smallest honest version; the old 5–10x needed blending. The advance over CacheWeaver is that a stateless counter matches its trie-greedy order, so no cache state is needed. Long-tail documents (23–60% of document tokens) still miss, so about 100% is not reachable.

label: V6:improve_g2
name: Popularity order with second-sighting cache writes
mech: Documents are still sent in order of descending global retrieval count from an online counter (ties broken by ID), with the system prompt first and the question last. Every hit is therefore an exact prefix match and the cached state is exact. Two changes fix the weak link. (1) Second-sighting admission. The client keeps a list of document-prefix hashes it has seen recently, with no cached state behind them. A cache breakpoint is placed only at prefix depths already seen within the TTL window. Documents past that depth go after the last breakpoint and are billed at 1.0x instead of a 1.25x write. This is the CDN "cache on second hit" / TinyLFU admission idea applied to breakpoint placement. (2) TTL by traffic regime. The 1-hour TTL (2x write cost) is used when the organisation sends fewer than about 1k requests per 5 minutes, and the 5-minute TTL otherwise. Replay setup: 100k chunks, top-5, Zipf, 4 breakpoints at document depths 2–5, Anthropic multipliers, compared with sending documents uncached. Bill ratios across 10 to 1,000 requests per 5 minutes: - Zipf 1.05: 1.06–1.24x - Zipf 1.2: 1.19–1.44x - Zipf 1.5: 1.46–1.83x The old always-write rule gave 0.88–1.61x and lost money at low traffic. The method now never loses in any tested regime, and 1.5x holds at Zipf 1.5 from about 100 requests per 5 minutes (1.66x), where the old rule needed about 1k. It covers document reordering only. Quality effect: only the reordering itself. Test it by comparing F1/EM and the spread across permutations against relevance order on a real model.
value: 1.06–1.83x cheaper per request than the best current API practice (documents uncached), with no approximated KV, and it runs client-side only. It no longer loses money at low traffic or flat popularity. Rarely retrieved documents still miss (23–60% of document tokens), so a hit rate near 100% is not reachable.
